common_name: Summer Sunset Plumleaf Azalea (Crown Estate Vivid Red Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a shaded ravine or woodland setting; Summer Sunset was chosen specifically for flower color that reads noticeably more saturated red than typical wild plumleaf azalea seedlings.

directions: Summer Sunset was selected by the Crown Estate Commissioners at Windsor for flowers of an unusually deep, saturated red that stand out among the naturally variable orange-to-red color range of wild plumleaf azalea populations along the Chattahoochee River Valley of Georgia and Alabama. Like the species, it withholds its display until mid to late summer, well after other rhododendrons have finished blooming, opening funnel-shaped flowers with long, showy stamens on the current season's growth. Site it at a shaded ravine edge or woodland margin in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil, since the species is naturally found along cool stream bottoms and colors hold best out of harsh afternoon sun. Once established, water only during prolonged summer dry spells, as the deep root system settles well into consistently moist, well-drained woodland soil.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Hohman was chosen for flowers running noticeably darker and more orange-toned than average wild-collected plumleaf azalea seedlings.

directions: Hohman commemorates influential Maryland nurseryman H. Lincoln Hohman, an early grower and promoter of rhododendron and azalea species in American gardens, and honors his role in bringing lesser-known southeastern natives like plumleaf azalea into wider cultivation. The selection was chosen for its deep reddish-orange flowers, a shade darker and warmer than the typical range of wild seedlings, opening in July and August on an upright, multi-stemmed shrub. Because plumleaf azalea naturally grows along shaded ravine bottoms in the Chattahoochee River Valley, give Hohman moist, humus-rich, strongly acidic soil and dappled woodland shade rather than open sun. Mulch heavily with pine bark or leaf litter to conserve the constant soil moisture this late-blooming species depends on through the heat of a Southern summer.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society

common_name: S. D. Coleman Plumleaf Azalea (Leach-Selected Vibrant Orange Form)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil at a woodland edge with dappled shade; this clone was later used by breeder David Leach as a parent in his July-blooming deciduous azalea hybrids for its especially vibrant color.

directions: S. D. Coleman was selected by hybridizer David Leach for its vibrant reddish-orange flowers, a clone distinctive enough that Leach later used it as a breeding parent for his July-flowering series of deciduous azalea hybrids. On its own the plant grows as a true, unhybridized plumleaf azalea, producing masses of funnel-shaped summer flowers with long, gracefully curved stamens that draw hummingbirds and swallowtail butterflies during the slow weeks of late July and August. Because the species is naturally confined to shaded ravines along the Chattahoochee River Valley of Georgia and Alabama, plant it in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil with morning sun and afternoon shade. Avoid summer drought stress and heavy pruning, since next year's flower buds are set on the current season's new growth by early fall.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society
David G. Leach, Rhododendrons of the World

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring into consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic soil at a pond margin, ditch bank, or rain garden; this old double-flowered form produces almost no viable seed and is propagated entirely from cuttings or division.

directions: The double swamp rose is a long-cultivated sport of the wild species with fully double, many-petaled pink flowers instead of the single five-petaled form typical of Rosa palustris, and it was already circulating in American and European gardens by the early 1800s before falling out of common cultivation for well over a century. Because the flowers are so packed with extra petals they set little to no seed, so plants are propagated exclusively from rooted stem cuttings or by digging and dividing an established sucker colony. Give it the same wet-tolerant siting as the wild swamp rose: full sun and constantly moist to seasonally flooded soil along a pond edge, ditch, or rain garden basin, where few other flowering shrubs can compete. The fragrant double blooms open over several weeks in early summer on arching, prickly canes, and established colonies spread slowly outward by root suckers.

common_name: Double Pasture Rose (var. nuttalliana, Historic Double-Flowered Form)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or suckers in spring into well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, sunny soil; this double-flowered heirloom form of pasture rose sets little seed and must be propagated from cuttings or transplanted suckers.

directions: This is a historic double-flowered form of the native pasture rose, once cultivated in Europe as early as the late 1700s under the name Rosa carolina var. nuttalliana before it disappeared from gardens there for decades and was later found still persisting in cultivation in the United States. Instead of the species' typical single five-petaled bloom, it opens crowded, many-petaled pink flowers that fade attractively toward white with age, appearing over a longer stretch of early summer than the wild form and sometimes producing a light repeat flush. Because the extra petals largely replace the reproductive parts, seed set is minimal, so new plants come from rooted cuttings or dug suckers rather than seed. Grow it exactly as the wild species prefers: full sun and lean, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil, where it forms a slowly spreading, drought-tolerant thicket useful for a sunny bank or historic rose collection.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Baltimore Belle Climbing Rose (1843 Hybrid Setigera Rambler)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring against a fence, arbor, or trellis in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to light shade; Baltimore Belle inherits the vigorous once-blooming climbing habit of its native prairie rose parent.

directions: Baltimore Belle was raised in 1843 by brothers Samuel and John Feast of Baltimore, Maryland, from a cross of the native climbing prairie rose with an old European Gallica rose, making it one of the earliest deliberately bred American climbing roses and a founding member of the once-popular Hybrid Setigera class. It carries forward the vigorous, arching-to-climbing cane structure and toughness of its wild Rosa setigera parent, but trades the species' single pink bloom for dense clusters of twenty or more small, cupped, blush-pink, sweetly fragrant double flowers in a single grand early-summer flush. Like its prairie rose parent it tolerates lean, average soil and considerable drought once established, needing only a sturdy fence, arbor, or old tree to scramble through. Prune only lightly right after bloom to remove dead or crowded canes, since flower buds form on the previous year's growth.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or early fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; this naturally occurring white-fruited form is the wild-type parent from which named selections like 'Duet' were later selected as sports.

directions: Callicarpa dichotoma f. albifructa is a naturally occurring white-berried form of purple beautyberry, distinct from the purple-fruited species in fruit color only, with the same arching branches, small pink summer flowers, and compact size around three to five feet. In fall the branches become lined with tight clusters of porcelain-white berries rather than the electric violet-purple of the typical species, giving a softer, almost ghostly display that shows up well against evergreen backdrops. It is the wild-type white form from which later branch-sport selections, including the variegated-leaf 'Duet', were themselves discovered and propagated, so growing the plain form preserves the un-variegated straight foliage alongside the white fruit. Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil with afternoon shade in warmer zones to prevent leaf scorch, and prune hard in late winter since flowers and fruit form only on new wood.
